title: The world, reviewed

cards: "The difference of your languages and colours." That phrase sits in the Qur'an's list of Allah's signs, right beside the creation of the heavens and the earth.
Languages and colors, counted as signs, like mountains and rain. Hold that next to the last stretch of this year. A circle of Sufi chanting in Senegal.
A youth group studying online on a weeknight. A Shia family in a hall of mourning in a big city. A convert at her first Friday prayer.
An imam in a small town who leads the prayer and then helps stack the chairs. A diverse, living ummah.

teach.h: MANY WAYS, EACH IN ITS OWN WORDS.
teach.b: The year met each group in its own words and ranked none. The Deobandi and Barelvi traditions of South Asia. The traveling preachers of the Tablighi Jamaat.
The Salafi approach, which seeks to follow the earliest generations closely, and is itself diverse. Sufi orders like the Tijaniyyah and the Muridiyyah.
Shia communities in Iraq, Lebanon, Iran and beyond, and the Isma'ilis with their living Imam. Converts, some of whom prefer the word reverts. Women speaking for themselves, and not all agreeing.
Young people, and Muslims living as minorities. Variety isn't a problem in the text.

teach.h: THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: The Qur'an says people were made into nations and tribes, in Pickthall's words, "that ye may know one another." Not that they may be identical: that they may meet and learn each other. What holds it together?

In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, the Prophet, peace be upon him, says the believers in their mercy and love for one another are like one body: when one part aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever.
Not one uniform. One body, with many parts that feel each other's pain. And on an ordinary day, a body knows about its far limbs.
A Muslim in Ohio hearing about a flood in Bangladesh, or a mosque fire in a town she'll never visit, is being asked by that hadith to feel it.

teach.h: LESS A MAP THAN A NERVOUS SYSTEM.
teach.b: The ummah is less a map than a nervous system.

how: Muslims pray for the wider ummah in their own words, and send aid to Muslim communities hit by disaster, sometimes through their local mosque.

games.q: the hadith compares the believers to a body. one part aches. what does the rest of the body do?
o: carries on as if nothing happened.
games.why: Sahih al-Bukhari: the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever. far limbs still belong to the body.

practice: Travel slowly, one breath per place: a mosque near you, a city in West Africa, a town in South Asia, a village in Indonesia, a family in a refugee camp, a student far from home, a convert praying alone in a small apartment.
If you pray, ask good for them in your own words; if you don't, simply let each place be real for a breath, full of people waking, working and praying.

wordCard.voice: The world. The ummah, the worldwide community of Muslims, many languages and colors, one body in the hadith's picture. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a community or nation; the ummah is the community of Muslims.

carryVoice: Your line: everywhere. When one part aches, the whole body feels it too. Until tomorrow.
